Meanwhile, every database faces a simple truth: disks are slow and memory is fast. A cache exploits that gap, holding hot rows close to the query path so repeated reads avoid costly trips into persistent storage on the disk below.

However, correctness complicates matters; a cache that serves stale rows can corrupt reports and decisions. Teams therefore pick an invalidation strategy: write through, write behind, or short expiry windows. Each choice trades freshness against speed; the right answer depends on how badly your users tolerate aged data. Warm cache hits delight; cold cache misses hurt.

Along with all that, most SQL tools hold a buffer pool: warm data blocks that sit in RAM. Sizing this pool wants craft, as a scrawny pool churns, but a giant pool robs RAM from joins, sorts, and background compaction tasks.

Finally, treat your cache as an optimization, not a crutch: fix bad queries first, add indexes, then call it done.
